"America's a home. We're an idea. But we also have been, and will continue to be, an argument." That's David Bobb on the 701 Civics podcast, and it's the heart of his new book with Tony Williams, Divided Over the Declaration. His central claim runs against the grain of how we usually talk about our differences: the argument over the Declaration of Independence isn't a sign of national weakness. It's a feature of American life, and always has been. From Frederick Douglass to Abraham Lincoln to Barbara Jordan, generation after generation has returned to the same document to ask the same question: are we living up to the promise that all are created equal? Douglass called the Declaration a promissory note. Lincoln called it the "apple of gold." Jordan, the lowest-ranking member of the Watergate committee, told the nation her faith in the Constitution was "total," even as she named that people like her were left out of it at the founding. The through-line, Bobb argues, is that returning to first principles is how a self-governing people works through its hardest disagreements. As Jordan put it, the task is not the elimination of disagreements, but the management of them. 🎧 Listen here:  https://bit.ly/4xuuNIx  #CivicsEducation  #DeclarationOfIndependence  #AmericanHistory  #CivicDiscourse  #BillOfRightsInstitute

A raccoon named Rebecca arrived at the White House as an ingredient. She was meant for the Thanksgiving dinner. Grace Coolidge adopted her instead. That small act says a lot about the woman. While her husband kept meetings short and words shorter, Grace opened the White House to the public, greeting visitors herself. She was the first First Lady to hold a bachelor's degree, taught at a school for the deaf, and welcomed Helen Keller to the presidential home more than once. When her son died in the summer of 1924, she kept her public appearances and let the country grieve alongside her rather than closing herself off. Respect, in her hands, was not a formality. It was how she treated people. This In Pursuit video is based on an essay by Colleen Shogan and produced with In Pursuit, an initiative of More Perfect. Free, under 4 minutes, with a companion lesson for grades 6-12. Watch:  https://lnkd.in/eT9p_5r4  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory  #SocialStudies  #FirstLadies  #TeachingResources

"Where flowers bloom, so does hope." Lady Bird Johnson said it, and she spent a lifetime acting on it. As the interstate system spread across the country in the 1960s, she looked at the billboards, junkyards, and overgrown roadsides and saw something bigger than an eyesore. She saw a loss of respect for the land itself. So she lobbied Congress and won. The Highway Beautification Act was nicknamed "Lady Bird's Bill." She launched community projects nationwide, helped spark the momentum that led to the first Earth Day in 1970, and insisted that beautification was "far more than a matter of cosmetics." To her, it was civic life: the effort to bring the natural and manmade worlds into harmony. This one comes with a special resonance. The essay behind the video was written by First Lady Laura Bush, herself a champion of conservation and libraries. December 1944. Bastogne, Belgium. Temperatures below 0. Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe and the 101st Airborne were surrounded, outnumbered 5 to 1, and running low on food, ammunition, and medicine. Then a letter arrived from the German commander. Surrender, it warned, or face "total annihilation." McAuliffe's reply was 1 word: "Nuts!" The Germans were baffled by the expression. The American officer who delivered the note translated it plainly: it meant go to hell. His men held the line for 6 more days until Patton's Third Army broke through. And that single word came to define a life built on courage. McAuliffe learned to parachute at 44. He jumped into Normandy. He helped develop the bazooka. He led from the front, shoulder to shoulder with troops half his age. BRI Vice President of Content Kirk Higgins tells the full story on this episode of Our American Stories, a reminder of what courage against overwhelming odds actually looks like. 🎧 Listen here:  https://ihr.fm/4yTuU1S  #CivicsEducation  #AmericanHistory  #WWII  #BattleOfTheBulge  #Courage  #BillOfRightsInstitute  #OurAmericanStories

"Leadership isn't just about rising in the ranks and stepping up when it's needed. It's also about stepping back, listening to people around you, and inspiring others to build themselves up." That's Bryce Herold, a high school debater from Ohio reflecting on 5 days at the Debate and Leadership Institute. Alongside Founding Forward, BRI brought rising 10th-12th graders to Valley Forge for a week of Socratic dialogue, debate workshops, and visits to Valley Forge National Historic Park and Independence Hall, culminating in a final tournament at the historic Union League of Philadelphia. The topic they debated: Whether Congress should be required to authorize deploying national security forces into states. No easy answers. That's the point. This is what civic education looks like when it's working 👇  https://bit.ly/4vScTy8  #CivicEducation  #Leadership  #DebateEducation  #Civics

President Johnson handed Grant the War Department, hoping he would hold the door open. Grant handed it back. In 1867, Andrew Johnson suspended Secretary of War Edwin Stanton and named Grant to fill the seat while Congress was out of session. Grant took it, but only to keep someone worse out. When the Senate voted to reinstate Stanton, Grant returned the office without a fight. Johnson attacked his character in public. Grant wrote back: "My honor as a soldier and integrity as a man have been violently assailed." He had chosen the law over the man who appointed him. The Monroe Doctrine wasn't written by James Monroe. John Quincy Adams drafted it, and he had spent his whole life preparing to. Paris at age ten. St. Petersburg as a teenage secretary. Minister to the Netherlands, then Prussia, then Russia. Secretary of State at 50. In 1821, he told a Fourth of July audience that America "goes not abroad, in search of monsters to destroy." 2 years later he built that principle into a presidential address that carried another man's name and shaped American foreign policy for the next 2 centuries. We toured George Washington's Mount Vernon home with the cast and crew of Young Washington  the estate where his ambition took shape. The film opens up a side of the founding father most people have never seen: not a distant myth, but a young man still becoming himself, a story each of us can recognize. Stand Together supported the film alongside Wonder Project, Angel Studios, George Washington's Mount Vernon, the Daniels Fund, and the Bill of Rights Institute. In theaters now.  #YoungWashington

The man who wrote the Constitution spent months arguing that the Bill of Rights was a bad idea. James Madison called written guarantees "parchment barriers." He thought a list of protected rights would leave every unlisted right exposed. Then, on June 8, 1789, he stood up in the First Congress and asked that body to pass one anyway. What changed his mind is the part most students never hear. It involved a promise he made on the campaign trail, a letter from a friend in Paris, and 2 states still refusing to ratify.
